INTRODUCTION
The question presented in this case is whether the
Second and Fourteenth Amendments protect the right
to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic
rifles. The AR-15 is “the most popular rifle in the country.” Smith & Wesson Brands, Inc. v. Estados Unidos
Mexicanos, 605 U.S. 280, 297 (2025). In District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008), this Court held
that the District of Columbia’s ban on the possession
of handguns violated the Second Amendment under
the two-step, text -then-history analysis the Court
later made “more explicit” in New York State Rifle &
Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 31 (2022).
Heller stands for the proposition that arms in common
use cannot be banned . That principle  requires the
same result here as in Heller: AR-15 platform and
similar semiautomatic rifles cannot be prohibited.
At the first step, Heller held that handguns are
“Arms” within the plain  text of the Second Amendment. “The 18th-century meaning” of that term “is no
different from the meaning today,” the Court explained: “weapons of offence, or armour of defence.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 581 (citation omitted). Therefore,
both a t the Founding and today, “all firearms ”—including, of course, handguns —“constituted ‘arm s.’ ”
Id. (citation omitted).
At the second step, Heller determined that there
was no historical justification for banning handguns.
“The sorts of weapons protected,” the Court concluded,
“were those ‘in common use at the time,’ ” a principle
that was “fairly supported by the historical tradition
of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual
weapons.’ ” Id. at 627 (citations omitted). Heller had
no difficulty concluding that handguns are in common

2
use and therefore protected. While the Court posited
several reasons why “a citizen may prefer a handgun
for home defense,” the dispositive fact was that “whatever the reason, handguns are the most popular
weapon chosen by American s for self-defense in the
home.” Id. at 629. It did not matter, as a dissent emphasized, that handguns also are “the overwhelmingly favorite weapon of armed criminals.” Id. at 682
(Breyer, J., dissenting). “The enshrinement of constitutional rights necessarily takes certain policy choices
off the table,” id. at 636, including prohibiting the possession of common arms. As the Court summarized its
decision in McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742
(2010), having “found that [the Second Amendment]
right applied to handguns” because of their common
use, it followed that “citizens must be permitted ‘to
use’ ” them, id. at 767–68 (citation omitted).
Applying Heller’s analysis  to this case, the outcome is clear—“the people” have a right to possess AR-
15 platform and  similar semiautomatic rifles . As a
matter of plain text,  such rifles are arms, just as all
other firearms are. As a matter of history, AR-15s and
similar semiautomatic rifles cannot be banned because they are in common use. There are many reasons why law-abiding citizens may prefer them: they
tend to be more accurate than handguns, to be lighter
weight and to produce less recoil than other types of
rifles or shotguns, and to have features such as pistol
grips and telescoping stocks that promote accuracy
and usability. But “[w]hatever the reason,” Heller, 554
U.S. at 629, tens of millions of Americans choose them
for lawful purposes like self- and home-defense, hunting, and target shooting, and they are legal to own in
a large majority of states across the country. Indeed,
in recent years they have been the second-best selling

3
type of firearm after handguns. Unless this Court is
prepared to limit the Second Amendment’s protection
to handguns—an untenable proposition—Heller’s reasoning compels recognizing the same protection  for
AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.
The courts below reached a different conclusion,
but their holdings  cannot be reconciled with Heller.
The Seventh Circuit held that Cook County’s ban does
not implicate the plain text of the Second Amendment.
Vir.Pet.App.4a–5a. Because the plain text covers all
firearms, that holding was error. The Second Circuit,
for its part, posited that  Connecticut’s ban is consistent with history because, in that court’s view, AR-
15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are “unusually dangerous weapons.” Grant.Pet.App.37a. But
under Heller, the decision whether a type of arm is too
dangerous for ordinary Americans to possess is one
that the people are  entitled to make, not one that
courts are empowered to make for them. That is the
fundamental principle animating the common use
test. Indeed, by any objective measure the handgun is
the most dangerous weapon to modern society . If we
were “constrained to use [Respondents’] rhetoric, we
would have to say that handguns are the quintessential ‘assault weapons’ in today’s society; they are used
far more often than any other kind of gun in violent
crimes.” Heller v. District of Columbia, 670 F.3d 1244,
1290 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (“Heller II”) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). Thus, if the Second Circuit’s analysis were
correct, Heller could not have come out the way that it
did.
Reversing the decisions below requires breaking
no new ground; this Court need only apply its holding
in Heller. But affirming the decisions below is

4
impossible without effectively overruling Heller and
severely limiting the Second Amendment’s protection.
For these reasons and those that follow, t his Court
should reverse the decisions below , hold that the
banned semiautomatic rifles are protected arms, and
remand for entry of judgment for Petitioners.1

STATEMENT OF THE CASE
I. The Rifle Is a Paradigmatic American
Arm.
On June 14, 1775, the Continental Congress resolved “[t]hat six companies of expert riflemen, be immediately raised in Pennsylvania, two in Maryland,
and two in Virginia,” to assist  in the siege of Boston .
See JOURNALS OF THE CONTINENTAL CONGRESS 1774–
1789, Vol. II. 1775 89 (1905). Writing to his wife Abigail, John Adams reported that Congress had approved raising “an excellent species of light infantry.
They use a peculiar kind of musket, called a rifle. It
has … grooves within the barrel, and  carries a ball
with great exactness to great distances. They are the
most accurate marksmen in the world .” CHARLES
FRANCIS ADAMS, FAMILIAR LETTERS OF JOHN ADAMS
AND HIS WIFE ABIGAIL ADAMS DURING THE REVOLU-
TION 65–66 (1876).
The Kentucky long rifle, named for the wilderness
area where it was employed most effectively, was
vastly more accurate than the traditional muskets of
the time, a feature  of critical importance to

6
frontiersmen who depended on them “to protect themselves and to provide themselves with food and clothing.” Stephen V. Grancsay, The Craft of the Early
American Gunsmith, 6 THE METROPOLITAN MUSEUM
OF ART BULLETIN 54, 54 (1947),
https://perma.cc/XS3G-74WS. Its accuracy resulted
from the “rifling” of the barrel, which causes a bullet
to spin through the air in a flatter, more accurate trajectory, id. at 56, similar to a football thrown in a tight
spiral. Musket barrels were not rifled and their ammunition “tumbled in flight” rather than traveling in
a controlled spin, id., more akin to a knuckleball pitch.
The Kentucky long rifle would earn an international reputation for American marksmen in the war.
At Saratoga, Tim Murphy, an American hunter and
rifleman “made General Fraser, one of the ablest British officers, his special target and wounded him mortally at a range of over three hundred yards,” id. at 54,
an impossible range to even attempt  with a musket ,
see H.C.B. RODGERS, WEAPONS OF THE BRITISH SOL-
DIER 93–94 (1960). And rifle technology continued to
develop. In 1777, Joseph Belton demonstrated  to
members of the Continental Congress  a repeating rifle, capable of firing multiple rounds without reloading, that could hold 16 rounds of ammunition. David
B. Kopel & Joseph G.S. Greenlee, The History of Bans
on Types of Arms Before 1900 , 50 J. LEGIS. 223, 255
(2024). Meriwether Lewis carried a Girandoni repeating air rifle, with a 22-round tubular magazine, on his
expedition with William Clark. JAMES B. GARRY,
WEAPONS OF THE LEWIS AND CLARK EXPEDITION 100–
01 (2012).
Throughout the 19th century, firearms technology
continued its advance , with repeating firearms

7
becoming increasingly commonplace. Samuel Colt received his first patent for a revolver in 1836, with Remington and Smith and Wesson also introducing models before the Civil War, all to great commercial success. Kopel & Greenlee, supra at 270–72. In the Civil
War, repeating rifles gained enormous popularity
both as military weapons and as tools of self -defense.
Id. at 278 (describing a Kentucky cavalry officer who
used a 16-shot Henry Rifle to kill seven Confederates
“who broke into his home and ambushed his family”).
And in the postbellum period, the 18-shot Winchester
Model 1866 and its successor th e Winchester Model
1873—“The Gun That Won the West”—were produced
in even greater numbers; by 1919 Winchester had
made over 720,000 Model 1873s alone. Id. at 279–80.
Semiautomatic firearm technology dates to  at
least 1885. Id. at 282. In the first decade of the 20th
century, popular models of semiautomatic rifle s and
shotguns hit the American market. See Heller II, 670
F.3d at 1287. Like their predecessors , they were
quickly adopted by the American people . While there
were a small number of laws enacted in the 1920s and
1930s that restricted semiautomatic firearms in some
ways, none amounted to a general ban on the technology. Rather, most states that enacted laws only  required permits, see 1933 Ohio Laws 189 –90, banned
possession for an “offensive or aggressive purpose,”
1934 Va. Acts 137–39, restricted magazine capacity of
firearms used in hunting, see, e.g., 1920 N.J. Laws 67,
ch. 31, § 9, or banned modifications of a firearm to increase its capacity, 1933 Minn. Laws ch. 190. Only two
states banned possession of some semiautomatic firearms, and in each case the ban applied only to  firearms above a certain ammunition capacity.  See 1927
Mich. Pub. Acts 888 –89 (16 rounds); 1927 R.I. Pub.

8
Laws 256 (12 rounds) . These outliers were  both repealed. See 1931 Mich. Pub. Acts 328, § 224; 1975 R.I.
Pub. Laws 738, 738 –39, 742. As this Court stated in
Staples v. United States , semiautomatic rifles “traditionally have been widely accepted as lawful possessions.” 511 U.S. 600, 612 (1994).
II. The AR-15 Is the Paradigmatic American
Rifle.
The AR-15 is “the ‘most popular rifle in American
history.’ ” Duncan v. Becerra, 970 F.3d 1133, 1148 (9th
Cir. 2020), rev’d on reh’g en banc , 19 F.4th 1087 (9th
Cir. 2021). It was developed by the ArmaLite corporation, from which it takes its name (“AR” for “ArmaLite
Rifle”) and originally produced by Colt . David B. Kopel, Machine Gun History and Bibliography, 25 WYO.
L. REV. 45, 103 (2025). When produced for the military
as a “selective fire rifle” that can operate as an automatic “machinegun,” it is most commonly known as
an M-16. Staples, 511 U.S. at 603. As a civilian firearm, the AR-15 became available in a semiautomatic
only form in the  1960s. See STEPHEN P. HALBROOK,
AMERICA’S RIFLE: THE CASE FOR THE AR-15 14–15
(2022). Unlike the M -16, the semiautomatic AR -15,
like all other semiautomatic firearms,  fires just one
round per pull of the trigger. See Garland v. Cargill ,
602 U.S. 406, 416 (2024).
When Colt’s patent lapsed in 1977, many companies began to produce rifles on the AR -15 platform—
just as many companies produced telephones after the
expiration of Alexander Graham Bell’s patents in
1894. See Adam D. Thierer , Unnatural Monopoly:
Critical Moments in the Development of the Bell System Monopoly, 14 CATO J. 267, 270 (1994). In the decades since, AR-15s have become enormously popular

9
“because they’re accurate, light , portable and modular.”  FRANK MINITER, THE FUTURE OF THE GUN 46–47
(2014). AR-15s are “e asy to shoot [with] little recoil,
making [them] popular with women, [and] … so user
friendly that a group called ‘Disabled Americans for
Firearms Rights’ ” recommends them for people who
find it physically difficult to  use other firearms. Id.
AR-15s in their ordinary configuration also are less
powerful than many older rifle designs. “The AR-15’s
smaller .223 … bullets strike with only one -fourth to
one-half of the energy of most other centerfire rifle
bullets,” and “some states ban the use of .223 caliber
rifles when hunting deer and other animals  larger
than varmints because their rounds lack sufficient
power.”  E. Gregory Wallace, “Assault Weapon” Lethality, 88 TENN. L. REV. 1, 53–54 (2020).2 These
rounds also generally “penetrate less through building materials than common handgun and shotgun
rounds.” Id. at 38; see also HALBROOK, supra at 398.
Indeed, the small size of the 5.56mm round (the military’s equivalent of the .223 round) led to continuous
complaints by soldiers  of the M16 being underpowered, leading the Army in 2022 to announce plans to
shift to a larger round. Kopel, Machine Gun History,
supra at 105–06.

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I. The plain text of the Second Amendment covers
Petitioners’ desired conduct  because t he challenged
laws ban the possession of AR-15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles, which are “arms.”
The Seventh Circuit faulted the Viramontes Petitioners for failing to show that semiautomatic rifles
such as the AR-15 are “arms.” But it did so by relying
on circuit precedent that improperly “smuggle[d] additional limits, drawn from our regulatory tradition,
into the plain -text stage of the inquiry.” Wolford v.
Lopez, 146 S. Ct. 2032, 2054 n.1 (2026) (Barrett, J.,
concurring).  As a matter of plain text, the term “arms”
extends at a minimum to “all firearms,” Heller, 554
U.S. at 581, and the Seventh Circuit was wrong to conclude otherwise.
II. A. At Bruen step two, there is no need for fresh
historical analysis because Heller already has set the
historical ground rules. “ The sorts of weapons protected” are those “in common use,” a limitation Heller
deemed “fairly supported by the historical tradition of
prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual
weapons.’ ” Id. at 627 (citations omitted).
Whatever common use may mean at the margins,
AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles fit squarely
within that category. Because “millions of Americans
own AR-15s and … a significant majority of the States
allow for possession of those rifles,” Snope v. Brown,
145 S. Ct. 1534, at 1534 (2025) (Kavanaugh, J., statement respecting denial of certiorari), it follows that
they “are commonly possessed by law-abiding citizens

for lawful purposes ,” Caetano v. Massachusetts , 577

Amendment.” Id.

empower courts to decide whether, according to
judges, a particular type of arm is “unusually dangerous.” But, under Heller, whether the danger posed by
a particular type of firearm outweighs its utility for
lawful purposes is a decision for the American people

145 S. Ct. at 1538 (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial
of certiorari). Furthermore, by definition, an arm in

Connecticut’s and Cook County’s Bans.
A. Under Heller, Law-Abiding Citizens
Have a Right to Possess AR-15s and
Similar Semiautomatic Rifles.
1. Because AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles are covered by the plain text of the Second Amendment, the burden shifts to Respondents to “demonstrate that the[ir] regulation[s]” banning such rifles
are “consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition
of firearm regulation.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 17. In a typical case, Respondents would need to establish the relevant tradition of regulation. In an arms ban case
such as this one, however, Heller already has conducted the historical analysis and “decided that the ‘in

29
common use’ test governs.” Mark W. Smith, What Part
of “In Common Use” Don’t You Understand?: How
Courts Have Defied Heller in Arms -Ban-Cases—
Again, PER CURIAM, HARV. J.L. & PUB. POL’Y (Sep. 27,
2023), https://perma.cc/Q6CA-CTH5.
Heller was just like this case, as it concerned a ban
on a type of firearm. After conducting its textual analysis, Heller turned its attention to history. Despite the
Second Amendment’s expansive phrasing, the Court
explained that the Amendment  does not protect “a
right to keep and carry any weapon whatsoever in any
manner whatsoever and for whatever purpose.” 554
U.S. at 626. Rather, Heller stated the right is subject
to historical limitations  and, as  relevant here, concluded “that the sorts of weapons protected [are] those
in common use.” Id. at 627 (quotation marks omitted).
The Court found this principle both “fairly supported
by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying
of dangerous and unusual weapons ,” id. (quotations
marks omitted), and consonant with the fact that “the
traditional militia was formed from a pool of men
bringing arms ‘in common use at the time’ for lawful
purposes like self-defense,” id. at 624. Thus, while the
government may be able to ban arms that are “highly
unusual in society at large ” and “not typically possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes,” id.
at 625, 627 , law-abiding citizens have an absolute
right to possess arms in common use for lawful purposes.
In McDonald, the Court reiterated what it held in
Heller. Heller, the Court explained,  “found that [the
Second Amendment] right applies to handguns because they are ‘the most preferred firearm in the nation to “keep” and use for protection of one’s home and

30
family.’ ” McDonald, 561 U.S. at 767 (quoting Heller,
554 U.S. at 628). And because handguns were in common use in this way,  the Court held that “citizens
must be permitted to use handguns for the core lawful
purposes of self-defense.” Id. at 768 (quotation marks
and brackets omitted).
Following McDonald, in Caetano v. Massachusetts, 577 U.S. 411 (2016) (per curiam), the Court summarily vacated a decision of the Supreme Judicial
Court of Massachusetts that departed from the common use test. The Massachusetts court had held that
stun guns are not protected by the Second Amendment because they “were not in common use at the
time of the Second Amendment’s enactment ” and are
not “readily adaptable to use in the military.” Id. at
411–12 (quotation marks omitted) . These rationales,
the Court explained, “contradict[] this Court’s precedent,” because Heller had expressly stated that the
Second Amendment reaches arms “that were not in
existence at the time of the founding ,” and had also
rejected the notion that “only those weapons useful in
warfare are protected.” Id. at 412 (quotation marks
omitted). While the per curiam majority focused on
the Massachusetts’ court’s errors, Justice Alito in concurrence identified the test that court should have applied: “whether stun guns are commonly possessed by
law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes today.” Id. at
420 (Alito, J., concurring).
Finally, in Bruen, this Court relied on the common
use principle for three distinct purposes. First , the
Court used it to illustrate how the Court in Heller had
“relied on the historical understanding of the Amendment to demark the limits on the exercise of the right.”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 21. “For example,” the Court

31
explained, “we found it ‘fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of “dangerous
and unusual weapons” ’ that the Second Amendment
protects the possession and use of weapons that are
‘in common use at the time.’ ” Id. (citation omitted).
Second, the Court held that the handguns at issue in
the case were protected arms—not just presumptively
protected, but protected full stop, as a matter of text
and history—because it was undisputed that “handguns are weapons ‘in common use’ today for self -defense.” Id. at 32. Third, the Court used the common
use principle to distinguish colonial laws that arguably barred the carry of handguns . “[E]ven if these colonial laws prohibited the carrying of handguns because they were considered ‘dangerous and unusual
weapons’ in the 1690s,” the Court reasoned, “they provide no justification for laws restricting the public
carry of weapons that are unquestionably in common

2. Heller not only establishes the common use
principle but also illustrates how the principle is to be
applied. The key insight is that “[o]ur constitution allows the American people … to decide which weapons
are useful for self-defense,” and therefore courts are to
“look[] to the standards set ‘by American society’ ”
when determining whether an arm is in common use.
Snope, 145 S. Ct. at 1537–38 (Thomas, J., dissenting).
“The scope of the right to bear arms cannot turn on
judicial speculation about the American people’s self -

Heller is clear that the common use test focuses on

it is permissible to ban the possession of handguns so

at 611–12. Such firearms “traditionally have been

The Court employed a similar mode of analysis in

4. Under this Court’s precedents, there can be no
doubt that AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic

While members of this Court have tended to focus

that tens of millions of Americans own them, with the

NSSF, Firearm Production, supra at 7.
Additionally, AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are legal in the vast majority of the

its further acknowledgment in Smith & Wesson, that

B. The Second Circuit’s Contrary Approach Is Inconsistent with Text,
History, and Precedent.
The Second Circuit below, unlike the Seventh ,
reached the historical analysis and resolved the case
on Bruen’s second step. But its reasoning was in direct
conflict with Heller and irreconcilable with our Nation’s history of firearm regulation.
1. In conducting its historical analysis, the Second
Circuit did not dispute that the banned rifles  are in
common use. Instead, the court rejected the common
use test altogether. “Even assuming, arguendo, that
the desired firearms and magazines are ‘typically possessed’ and ‘in common use’ for lawful purposes,’ ” the
court reasoned, that would not be “ ‘sufficient’ for finding that possessing the regulated weapons is protected by the Second Amendment.”
Grant.Pet.App.29a-30a. That conclusion cannot be
reconciled with this Court’s precedents , and t his
Court could reject the Second Circuit’s holding on that
basis alone.
The Second Circuit claimed that Petitioners were

relies,” id. at 30a, but, respectfully, it was the Second
Circuit doing the distorting, not Petitioners. The court
insisted that this Court’s “cases do not hold that the

37
Second Amendment necessarily protects all weapons
in common use,” and therefore “ [t]hey do not shield
popular weapons from review of their potentially unusually dangerous character.” Id. But this Court’s
cases do exactly that. In Heller, for example, the Court
held that handguns cannot be banned precisely because they “are the most popular weapon chosen by
Americans for self -defense in the home.” 554 U.S. at
629. The popularity of handguns was sufficient to resolve the case. The Court did not go on to examine
whether handguns nevertheless had an “unusually
dangerous character, ” Grant.Pet.App.30a,  despite
Justice Breyer’s dissent arguing just that, i.e., that
handguns have “attributes” that “make them particularly dangerous,” id. at 711 (Breyer, J., dissenting).
The issue was simply irrelevant. Bruen was much the
same. There, because there was no “dispute that
handguns are weapons ‘in common use’ today for selfdefense,” there was nothing more the Court needed to

597 U.S. at 32.
The Second Circuit further found it relevant that
Connecticut’s ban “leave[s] open many lawful alternatives to Connecticut residents for armed self-defense.”
Grant.Pet.App.46a. This reasoning too is foreclosed by
Heller. There, D.C. emphasized that its handgun ban
allowed its citizens to possess shotguns and rifles,
“which some gun rights proponents contend are actually the weapon of choice for home defense.” Br . for
Pet’rs, 2008 WL 102223, at *54–55, District of Columbia v. Heller , No. 07 -290 (Jan. 4, 2008)  (citing Clint

The Court rejected this argument, reasoning that “it

38
permissible to ban the possession of handguns so long

sounder when rifles are being banned.
The Second Circuit acknowledged that its reasoning was in tension with Justice Alito’s concurrence in
Caetano stating that “[a] weapon may not be banned
unless it is both dangerous and unusual,” 577 U.S. at
417 (Alito, J., concurring), but it discounted that opinion as a “non -binding concurrence,”
Grant.Pet.App.32a. Caetano cannot be dismissed so
easily, however. As Justice Alito explained, “as the per
curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test.”
Caetano, 577 U.S. at 417 (Alito, J., concurring) (emphasis added). The per curiam did so by summarily
vacating the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court’s
judgment after concluding that the court’s assessment

The Second Circuit additionally protested that the

them.” Grant.Pet.App.30a. (cleaned up). Here too, the
Second Circuit’s reasoning already has been rejected

at 720–21 (Breyer, J., dissenting).

39
The Second Circuit also is wrong that the common
use test turns the analysis into a trivial counting exercise. Rather, the key question is whether the people
have deemed an arm to be a dangerous and unusual
weapon. To be sure, in answering that question, the
number of a type of arm owned by the American people may be highly relevant. But that is because when,
as in this case, tens of millions of Americans across
the country own a type of arm for lawful purposes, it
is impossible to conclude that  the people have determined the arm is so dangerous it is unfit for use by
ordinary citizens. Absurd hypotheticals about nuclear
weapons are just that—absurd. “Even if some nuclear
warheads are small enough for an individual to carry,
no reasonable person would think to use one to defend
himself.” Snope, 145 S. Ct. at 1538 (Thomas, J., dissenting). “To fend off the fantastical threat  of Americans lobbing nuclear warheads at one another,” the
Second Circuit “has allowed the very real threat of the
government depriving Americans of the rifle that they
most favor for protecting themselves and their families.” Id.
By insisting that there is still work to be done beyond common use, the Second Circuit revealed the
true principle at work in its reasoning —that even
though there are some arms that the people, by their
actions, have determined are appropriate to possess
and use, there nevertheless remains room for judges
to override them if judges think that a common type
of arm is “too dangerous. ” This reasoning is fundamentally incompatible with this Court’s Second
Amendment jurisprudence. As Heller explained,
“[t]he very enumeration of the right takes out of the
hands of government—even the Third Branch of Government—the power to decide on a case-by-case basis

40
whether the right is really worth insisting upon.” 554
U.S. 63 4. The Court therefore has rejected means -
end-scrutiny in favor of an approach focused on history, and it has made clear that courts cannot “engage
in independent means -end scrutiny under the guise
of” historical inquiry. See Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29 n.7.
Here, the relevant historical principle is that arms
that are in common use cannot be banned. Courts
therefore have no basis for considering “difficult empirical” questions of the type that the Second Circuit’s
approach raises, McDonald, 561 U.S. at 791 (plurality), such as “what sorts of guns are necessary for selfdefense,” id. at 923 (Breyer, J., dissenting), how dangerous AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are relative to other firearms, and the extent to
which the attributes of those rifles make them attractive to criminals.  This kind of interest balancing is
foreclosed by Heller and Bruen. Rather, it is the “balance struck by the traditions of the American people”
that bind the courts.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 26 (em-dash
omitted).
2. Having rejected Heller’s common use standard,
the Second Circuit proceeded to engage in its own historical analysis , supplemented by a concurrence by
Judge Nathan that the court “fully join [ed],”
Grant.Pet.App.33a, to arrive at the conclusion that
unusually dangerous arms can be banned.
Before getting to the substance of the Second Circuit’s analysis, it is important to note that the analysis
was marked by significant methodological errors.
First, the court posited that “because the challenged statutes are state laws, the prevailing understanding of the right to bear arms in both 1791 … and
1868 … are relevant to our analysis.”

41
Grant.Pet.App.36a. While this Court has not resolved
whether the prevailing understanding in 1791 or 1868
controls, it has “made clear that individual rights enumerated in the Bill of Rights and made applicable

the Federal Government and States is pegged to the

Rights was adopted in 1791.” Id. (collecting cases).
Second, the court posited that “a nuanced analysis” was required “because the challenged legislation
addresses novel societal problems stemming from
newly developed technology.” Grant.Pet.App.38a. The
court pointed to mass shootings as such a problem .
But Heller and Bruen both involved a “straightforward historical inquiry,” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27, not a
more nuanced one, despite the issue of mass shootings
being raised in both, see, e.g., Br. of Violence Pol’y Ctr.
et al. as Amici Curiae Supporting Pet’rs , 2008 WL
136348, at *24, District of Columbia v. Heller, No. 07-
290 (Jan. 11, 2008) ; Bruen, 597 U.S. at 132 (Breyer,
J., dissenting). Indeed, Heller involved the weapon of
choice for mass shooters, the handgun . See Rosanna

RAND (updated Jan. 29, 2026),
https://perma.cc/L7YX-BG4E). And Bruen involved
carrying handguns in public, where the concern about
mass shootings is most acute . Yet neither case  required a nuanced analysis because of the existence of
mass shootings.

42
The Second Circuit’s assessment of dramatic technological change fares no better. AR-15 platform and
similar semiautomatic rifles do represent a technological advance over Founding-era rifles, but they have
been on the market for nearly sixty years , and they
rely on semiautomatic technology that is over a hundred years old.  And here, again, this case cannot require nuance when Heller and Bruen were straightforward, as the handguns at issue in those cases were
just as different from Founding-era handguns as modern rifles are different from their Founding-era counterparts. Cf. Snope, 145 S. Ct. at 1534 (Kavanaugh, J.,
statement respecting denial of certiorari).
In any event, whether this case is categorized as
straightforward or nuanced ultimately is of little moment. “The Court’s note about the occasional need for
a ‘more nuanced approach’ was an unremarkable observation that making comparisons to proper historical analogies might be challenging at times,” Duncan
v. Bonta, 133 F.4th 852, 910 (9th Cir. 2025) (en banc)
(Bumatay, J., dissenting), not an invitation to fundamentally alter the analysis in cases concerning distinctly modern issues. See also ANJRPC, 183 F.4th at
246; J. Joel Alicea, Bruen  Was Right , 174 U. PA. L.
REV. 13, 32 n.144 (2025) . And here, the common use
principle itself accounts for social and technological
changes resulting from advancements in firearms
technology. The controlling question here is whether
a given type of arm is “in common use today.” Bruen,
597 U.S. at 47 (emphasis added). The inquiry therefore is one that accounts for the American people’s
judgment regarding what sorts of arms are appropriate for typical, lawful possession according to contemporary social and technological conditions. Any nuance required already is accounted for in  the

43
controlling constitutional standard. See, Smith, Common Use, supra at 17.
3. The Second Circuit’s historical analysis began
with the practice of restricting the carrying of “dangerous and unusual weapons,” but it drew the wrong
lessons from that historical practice , by concluding
that this tradition justifies banning “those arms that
legislators determined were unusually dangerous because of their characteristics.” Grant.Pet.App.31a.
As explained above, Heller stated that its holding
that “the sorts of weapons protected were those in
common use” was “fairly supported by the historical
tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and
unusual weapons.’ ” 554 U.S. at 627. Looking at the
sources cited by Heller for this proposition, the Second
Circuit noted that they “use a mix of ‘dangerous or unusual’ and ‘dangerous and unusual ’ ” to describe the
weapons covered. Grant.Pet.App.70a (Nathan, J., concurring). But this variation does not support the conclusion that arms in common use can be banned if the
government deems them unusually dangerous.
A principal primary source for the historical understanding of restrictions on carrying dangerous and
unusual weapons is Serjeant William Hawkins’
“widely read” Treatise on the Pleas of the Crown. See
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 45. While Heller’s string cite on this
issue did not include Hawkins, many of those sources
themselves relied on his treatise. See, e.g., 4 WILLIAM
BLACKSTONE, COMMENTARIES ON THE LAWS OF ENG-
LAND 148 (1769); 3 B. WILSON, WORKS OF THE HONOUR-
ABLE JAMES WILSON 79 (1804). Hawkins’ discussion of
dangerous and unusual weapons is contained within
his broader discussion of affrays . The word “affray ,”
Hawkins explained, was “derived from the French

44
word” meaning “to terrify,” and “in a legal Sense, it is
taken for a publick  Offence, to the Terror of the People.” 1 WILLIAM HAWKINS, TREATISE ON THE PLEAS OF
THE CROWN 134 (1716). As such, “there may be an Assault which will not amount to an Affray; as where it
happens in a private Place ,” because in such a  “Case
it cannot be said to be to the Terror of the People.” Id.
While an affray typically involved some sort of “actual
Violence,” that was not always so, such as “where a
Man arms himself with dangerous and unusual Weapons, in such a manner as will naturally cause a Terror
to the People.”  Id. at 135. This behavior, Hawkins
stated, was “said to have been always an Offense at
Common Law, and is strictly prohibited by many Statutes,” most prominently the 1328 Statute of Northampton. Id. Hawkins made clear, however, “that no
wearing of Arms is within the meaning of this statute,
unless it be accompanied with such Circumstances as
are apt to terrify the People.” Id. at 136. And from
that, “it seems clearly to follow, that Persons of Quality are in no Danger of Offending against this Statute
by wearing common Weapons … for their Ornament
or Defence, in such Places, and upon such Occasions,
in which it is the common Fashion to make use of
them, without causing the least Suspicion of an Intention to commit any Act of Violence or Disturbance of
the Peace.” Id. As Bruen explains, the historical evidence indicates that “the founding generation” shared
the understanding that the “in Terrorem Populi” element “require[d] something more than merely carrying a firearm in public.” 597 U.S. at 50.
What should be immediately apparent from Hawkins’ discussion is that the affray tradition was one
principally regulating public conduct, not conduct in
the home. Because the affray tradition concerned

45
public behavior, a person generally could commit a
“dangerous and unusual weapons”  offense in two
ways: by carrying a weapon that was so dangerous
and so unusual that its mere presence signified an intent to breach the peace, or by carrying a more common weapon in a manner that signified such an intent. With respect to the former, Bruen discusses
launcegays, which in 14th Century England “were
generally worn or carried only when one intended to
engage in lawful combat or … to breach the peace.”
597 U.S. at 41. With respect to the latter, a good illustration is provided by the North Carolina Supreme
Court’s decision in State v. Huntly, 25 N.C. 418 (1843).
There, the court affirmed a conviction under the common law affray tradition against an individual who
rode in public “armed with a double barrelled gun”
while threatening to kill several fellow citizens. Id. at
419. In affirming the conviction, the court explained
that “the carrying of a gun per se constitutes no offense. For any lawful purpose … the citizen is at perfect liberty to carry his gun.” Id. at 422–23. But that
did not authorize a citizen to carry a firearm “to terrify
and alarm, and in such manner as naturally will terrify and alarm, a peaceful people.” Id. at 423.
Perhaps the fact that an affray could sometimes
be committed by behaving in a manner threatening to
the public, even if the affrayer were doing so with a
common weapon, explains why it was sometimes articulated as applying to either “dangerous and unusual” weapons or to “dangerous or unusual” weapons.
This case, however, concerns a flat ban on possession
even in the home. While Heller said that the tradition
of banning dangerous  and unusual arms “fairly supported” bans on mere possession, see 554 U.S. at 627,
such a conclusion only makes sense as applied to arms

46
that are both highly dangerous and highly unusual.
There is no basis for inferring an intent to commit violence—and therefore to terrify the publi c—from the
simple possession in the home of  a common firearm ,
especially when the constitution protects a fundamental right to keep and bear arms. Cf. Simpson v. State,
13 Tenn. 356, 360 (1833).  Heller thus properly described unprotected arms as “highly unusual in society at large” and “not typically possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes.” 554 U.S. at 625, 627.
This conclusion is not based on a “first intuition about
the word ‘and,’ ” Grant.Pet.App.72a (Nathan, J., concurring), but rather on the foundational principles underlying the Second Amendment protected right.

Circuit next pointed to laws “targeting unusually dangerous, novel, and concealable weapons, including
uniquely configured dirk and Bowie knives .”
Grant.Pet.App.53a.
There are  several p roblems with analogizing to
these laws. First, these laws date, at the earliest, to
1837, see Kopel & Greenlee, supra at 296–327, which
is too late to inform the understanding of the right
that was enshrined in the Constitution in 1791. See
ANJRPC, 183 F.4 th at 231–32. “Post-ratification
adoption or acceptance of laws that are inconsistent
with the ori ginal meaning of the constitutional text
obviously cannot overcome or alter that text.” Bruen,
597 U.S. at 36 (quoting Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1274 n.6
(Kavanaugh, J., dissenting)).
Second, while many states enacted laws that restricted Bowie knives in some way, the restrictions
were almost always less severe than the bans at issue
here. “Most of those regulations prohibited the

47
concealed carry of Bowie knives, and some prohibited
open carry with intent to do harm or imposed more
stringent punishments where Bowie knives were used
in the commission of a crime.” ANJRPC, 183 F.4th at
244; see id. at nn.37–40 (collecting laws); see also Teter
v. Lopez, 76 F.4th 938, 951–53 (9th Cir. 2023), vacated
as moot on reh’g en banc , 125 F.4th 1301 (9th Cir.
2025). The Second Circuit cited a few restrictions that
went further by restricting both open and concealed
carry, placing a prohibitive tax on Bowie knives, or, in
the case of one Tennessee law, “outright bann[ing] the
sale of such weapons .” Grant.Pet.App.55a–56a. But
the 1837 Georgia law that the panel said “forbade the
sale, possession, or carry of dirk and Bowie knives,”
Grant.Pet.App.56a n.37, exempted open carry of such
weapons, 1837 Ga. Acts 90, § 4. And the rest were outliers that provide little insight into “the general understanding of [the] codified right.” Wolford, 146 S. Ct.
at 2050.
Third, the laws regulating the carry of Bowie
knives are in the same vein as (and often are the same
laws as) those regulating the carry of handguns that
this Court found insufficient to support banning possession of handguns in Heller or restricting their public carry in Bruen. Take the Georgia law discussed
above. Unlike Bowie knives, that law did ban carrying
handguns both openly and concealed. And, in an opinion cited approvingly in Heller, it was held to be unconstitutional to the extent it banned open  carry. See
Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243, 251 (1846); see also Heller,
554 U.S. at 612. Additionally, laws that did restrict
both open and concealed carry of Bowie knives  similarly restricted the carry of handguns (with exceptions
in Arkansas for types of handguns used in the military). See 1881 Ark. Acts 191; 1871 Tex. Gen. Laws

48
25, 25 –27. If these laws were insufficient to justify
New York’s “good cause” requirement to carry handguns in public, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 64–65 (rejecting
the Texas law as an “outlier[]”); id. at 69 n.31 (citing
Arkansas law), they must be insufficient to justify
banning possession of an arm altogether.
Fourth, unlike AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles, it is not clear that Bowie knives were
“in common use” at the time they were banned . See
United States v. Bridges, 150 F.4th 517, 537 (6th Cir.
2025) (quotation marks omitted) (Nalbandian, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment) . To
the extent laws restricting Bowie knives or other arms
were examined by courts at the time and held to be
constitutional, it generally was because courts
“tracked a distinction we’ve seen before: that between
dangerous and unusual weapons and common weapons.” Bianchi v. Brown , 111 F.4th 438, 51 0 (4th Cir.
2024) (Richardson, J., dissenting). Assessing four such
cases from Texas, Arkansas, and Tennessee, Judge
Richardson noted that “all four courts assessed the
challenged statutes according to the same principle.
Each of them determined whether the regulated
weapon was in common use for lawful purposes. If it
was, then they held that the government could regulate the possession or carry of that weapon, but that it
could not completely ban it.” Id. (discussing State v.
Duke, 42 Tex. 455, 456–59 (1875); Fife v. State, 31 Ark.
455 (1876); Andrews v. State, 50 Tenn. 165 (1871); and
Aymette v. State, 21 Tenn. 154 (1840)).
5. The Second Circuit finally turned for support to
“twentieth-century regulation of automatic and semiautomatic weapons.” Grant.Pet.App.58a. But semiautomatic restrictions were  exceedingly rare, were, in

49
the few cases in which they amounted to an actual
ban, restrictions on capacity, not on semiautomatic
firearms themselves, and were short lived. See supra
at 7–8. Furthermore, these laws, which all post -date
the New York law held unconstitutional in Bruen, are
far too late to inform our understanding of the scope
of the Second Amendment protected right to keep and
bear arms, especially in light of the total lack of support for the Second Circuit’s principle at any earlier
period in our history.
6. For these reasons, the Second Circuit’s attempt
to find historical support for banning “unusually dangerous” weapons fails. But even if it succeeded, that
would not change the outcome of this case. As an initial matter, because the banned rifles are in common
use, they are not unusually dangerous. They also are
not inherently more dangerous than other comparable
firearms. “AW-type firearms do not operate differently than other semiautomatics, nor do they fire
more lethal ammunition.” Christopher S. Koper, Assessing the Potential to Reduce Deaths and Injuries
from Mass Shootings Through Restrictions on Assault
Weapons and Other High -Capacity Semiautomatic
Firearms, 19 CRIM. & PUB. POL’Y 147, 149 (2020). To
the extent the features singled out by Connecticut and
Cook County—such as pistol grips, thumbhole stocks,
and telescoping stocks—make a difference, they do so
by promoting accuracy and therefore safety in using a
firearm, not danger. There is no historical warrant for
considering firearms with accuracy enhancing features to be unusually dangerous. In any event, “whatever the reason,” the people of this Nation overwhelmingly choose AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles for ordinary and lawful uses  and,

50
therefore, “a complete prohibition of their use is invalid.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 629.
CONCLUSION
This Court should reverse the decisions below and
remand with instruction s that judgment be entered
for Petitioners in both cases.
